issues.location: 'A list is an array with a counter', new paragraph right after the CS1612 code block: 'The same line compiles against an array, because T[]'s indexer does return by reference...'
issues.problem: Terminology looseness introduced this round. C#'s 'indexer' is a specific language feature (a this[] property backed by get_Item/set_Item), which is exactly what List<T> has and what the preceding sentences correctly describe. Array element access (a[i]) is not implemented as an indexer at all -- it is a built-in language construct (IL ldelema/ldelem) that the C# specification classifies as a variable, which is why it is assignable in place. Calling it 'T[]'s indexer' blurs the very distinction the paragraph is making: the reason List<T>[i].Field = x fails and array[i].Field = x succeeds is not that one indexer returns by value and another 'indexer' returns by reference, it is that only one of the two is an indexer (a method call) at all; the other is direct variable access. The underlying behavioral claim is correct and independently verified (both examples compile/fail exactly as stated) -- only the label is imprecise.
issues.fixLooksLike: Replace 'because T[]'s indexer does return by reference' with something like 'because array element access is not an indexer at all -- the compiler treats a[i] as a variable, the same as a field, so it can be assigned into directly' -- or, more simply, 'because a[i] is a variable, not a method call, unlike List<T>'s indexer.'
